questions.explain: Query Store persists query plans and runtime statistics across restarts, which sys.dm_exec_query_stats cannot do.
questions.q: Which SQL Server feature persists query plans and runtime statistics across service restarts, filling the gap left by sys.dm_exec_query_stats?

questions.explain: In sys.dm_exec_query_stats, high total_elapsed_time with low total_worker_time means the query is waiting — on locks, I/O, or the network — not doing CPU work.
options: The query is waiting on locks, I/O, or the network
The query is using too many parallel threads
questions.q: In sys.dm_exec_query_stats, what does high total_elapsed_time with low total_worker_time indicate?

questions.explain: PAGEIOLATCH_SH indicates a buffer pool miss reading from disk; sustained high values mean the working set exceeds memory or storage is slow.
questions.q: Which wait type indicates buffer pool misses reading from disk, suggesting the working set exceeds available memory?

questions.explain: If signal_wait_time_ms is more than 15–20% of total wait time, the chapter says you have CPU pressure.
questions.q: If signal_wait_time_ms is a significant fraction (15–20%+) of total wait time, what does the chapter say you have?

questions.explain: sys.dm_os_wait_stats accumulates cumulative waits; the recommended approach is to take delta snapshots over a meaningful interval (e.g., 60 seconds during peak load) and compute each type's percentage of total wait time.
options: Query it once and sort by wait_time_ms
Only look at the maximum wait time
Take delta snapshots over an interval and compute each wait type's percentage of total wait time
questions.q: What is the recommended way to analyze sys.dm_os_wait_stats to find the real bottleneck?
